source.title: HerBERT: Efficiently Pretrained Transformer-based Language Model for Polish
source.authors: Robert Mroczkowski; Piotr Rybak; Alina Wróblewska; Ireneusz Gawlik

record.tranche_reason: The study varies corpus size and pretraining length and measures downstream KLEJ performance, but does not measure held-out pretraining loss or reproduce a scaling-law fit.
record.gate_note: The study reports downstream KLEJ scores for corpus-size and pretraining-length comparisons. It does not report held-out cross-entropy losses, parameter-count or compute sweeps, scaling-law fits, or compute-optimal allocations. Results cited from Kaplan et al. are not this study's results and are excluded.
record.test_reason: A new setting: Polish BERT-base continued from XLM-R weights. The study compares downstream KLEJ scores for Small vs Large corpus and for 10k vs 50k pretraining iterations, so it bears on whether downstream performance improves with data or training scale (V6). Only two points per comparison, no loss measurement and no fit, so it can show direction but not predictability.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also conclude that SSO is not beneficial and that BPE-Dropout does not improve quality. They stress that multilingual initialization, not training length, let HerBERT beat Polish RoBERTa despite about ten times shorter training.
record.recipe_differences: A limited downstream-performance ablation over corpus size and training iterations, rather than a held-out-loss scaling-law study or compute-optimal allocation sweep.
record.method_sensitivity: Corpus-size differences in downstream score depend on SSO weight and BPE-Dropout setting; pretraining-length comparisons also change the learning-rate schedule.
record.peer_reviewed: Workshop on Balto-Slavic Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The evidence for V6 is limited to downstream KLEJ averages, a small number of corpus and iteration settings, and no scaling-law fit. The 10k-to-50k comparison also changes the learning rate schedule. Scores are averages over the six KLEJ tasks with validation sets, not per-task scaling results.
record.rows_left_out: Other ablation results (initialization, SSO weight, BPE-Dropout) and final benchmark comparisons do not measure corpus-size or training-length trends relevant to the tested V6 claim; cited scaling-law findings are not this study's results.

untested.parts: Predictability (trend or fit) across many scales; scaling with parameter count in a controlled sweep; prediction from pretraining loss; scratch-trained models (all ablation runs start from XLM-R).
Held-out loss vs parameters, tokens or compute: not measured.
Shape at fixed parameter count: not tested.
No power-law form in any regime; the transfer initialization is used but not scaled.

missing.what: BASE vs LARGE model-size comparison on downstream tasks. LARGE beats BASE on KLEJ average for all three model families (HerBERT 88.4 vs 86.3), but HerBERT BASE beats LARGE on CDSC-E. In dependency parsing, HerBERT LARGE UAS (95.11) is below BASE (95.18). Confounded by different training lengths and schedules.

record.verdict_notes: Evidence for V6 is weak: continued pretraining from XLM-R, downstream averages near ceiling (~89), two points per comparison. The corpus-size comparison holds training tokens fixed (10k iterations, batch 2560), so it tests unique-data quantity and repetition rather than scale of training. The finding that initialization beats around 10x more training across models is a cross-model, confounded comparison, not recorded as a verdict.

versions.untested_parts: Power-law held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger runs from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations and their trends with compute.
Effects of architecture shape at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes; multilingual-to-monolingual initialization is used, but no scaling law is measured.
The study tests downstream performance against corpus size and pretraining iterations only. It does not test model size, compute, or predictability from pretraining loss, nor a broad range of scales.
No exponents, compute-optimal split, or scaling-curve fit-dependence is evaluated.

relationships.condition: 10k vs 50k pretraining iterations (5x training tokens), SSO weight 1.0 and 0.1, Large corpus
relationships.reason: Longer training gives small but statistically significant KLEJ gains (r10 89.43 vs 89.10; r12 89.87 vs 89.37). Direction only, from two points, confounded by a learning-rate change.
relationships.display_finding: Longer training produced statistically significant KLEJ gains from 89.10 to 89.43 and 89.37 to 89.87, although the comparison also changed the learning rate.

relationships.condition: Small (1.66B) vs Large (8.6B tokens) corpus at fixed 10k iterations, across SSO/BPE-Dropout settings
relationships.reason: Large is numerically higher in all four settings but significant only for SSO 1.0 with BPE-Dropout (r2); r4, r6 and r8 are non-significant. The authors say a benefit is not obvious.
relationships.display_finding: The 8.6B-token corpus numerically outperforms 1.66B tokens in all four settings, but the gain is significant only with SSO 1.0 and BPE-Dropout.
